kurals.tamil:
அறவினை யாதெனின் கொல்லாமை கோறல்
பிறவினை எல்லாந் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Aravinai yaadhenin kollaamai koral
Piravinai ellaam tharum.
kurals.meaning: If you ask what virtuous action is, it is not killing any living being; killing, in turn, brings every other kind of evil deed in its wake.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a row of dominoes. If you knock over the first one, all the others fall too. Valluvar says killing is that first domino: once someone is willing to take a life, every other bad act becomes easy. Not killing keeps the whole row standing.
kurals.university: Valluvar answers the question “what is aram (virtue)?” with a single negative act — kollaamai, abstention from killing — and then gives its mirror image: kōṟal (killing) “yields all other deeds” (piṟavinai), which the classical commentators, including Mu. Varadarasan, read as all non-virtuous deeds. The couplet therefore makes non-killing not merely one virtue among many but the generative root of the moral life, with killing as the root of vice. This places the Kural squarely within the broad śramaṇic and Brahmanical consensus of early-first-millennium India that ahiṃsā is the highest dharma, a position shared by Jain, Buddhist and epic Hindu sources. The structure of the verse — definition followed by its contrary — is typical of Valluvar’s aphoristic logic, compressing an entire ethical theory into seven words.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Abstention from injury is the highest religion.”
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata’s Anushasana Parva, Bhishma teaches Yudhishthira that ahimsa (non-injury) is the supreme dharma — the famous formula ahimsa paramo dharmah.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s answer to “what is virtue?”: non-killing is virtue in its highest form.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section CXV (K. M. Ganguli trans.)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verbatim from Ganguli’s translation on sacred-texts.com; near one-to-one match with the Kural’s definition of aram.

christianity.explanation: The sixth commandment in the Decalogue given at Sinai forbids the unlawful taking of human life.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it places the prohibition on killing at the foundation of the moral law.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match in spirit; the biblical command concerns human life (murder), whereas Valluvar’s kollaamai extends to all living beings.

islam.quote_or_event: “whoever kills a soul unless for a soul or for corruption [done] in the land - it is as if he had slain mankind entirely. And whoever saves one - it is as if he had saved mankind entirely.”
islam.explanation: After the story of Adam’s two sons, the Qur’an declares that unjustly killing one person is morally equivalent to killing all humanity.
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat killing as the gravest of wrongs, one that contains the seed of every other evil.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on quran.com; strong match, though the verse allows exceptions (retribution, corruption) and concerns human life, while the Kural is unqualified and covers all creatures.

judaism.quote_or_event: “if any man has caused a single life to perish from Israel, he is deemed by Scripture as if he had caused a whole world to perish; and anyone who saves a single soul from Israel, he is deemed by Scripture as if he had saved a whole world.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah explains why God created a single human first: to teach that each life is an entire world.
judaism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s conviction that taking a life is not one wrong among many but a total, world-destroying wrong.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; strong thematic match, but scoped to human life (and in the printed text, to Israel), not to all living beings.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All tremble at violence; all fear death. Putting oneself in the place of another, one should not kill nor cause another to kill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha grounds the precept against killing in empathy: every creature fears death just as we do.
buddhism.tie_back: Same core teaching as the Kural — non-killing is the basic ethical act from which the rest of goodness flows.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified on Access to Insight; near one-to-one match, covering all beings as the Kural does.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Orestes, having killed his mother Clytemnestra, is hounded across Greece by the Furies (Erinyes), who pursue bloodguilt relentlessly until he is tried at Athens.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aeschylus’ Eumenides the spilling of kindred blood unleashes a chain of pursuit, madness and pollution that no one can escape by ordinary means.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Echoes the Kural’s second line: one killing sets in motion a whole train of further evils.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; thematic parallel on the cascading consequences of bloodshed, though Greek myth focuses on kin-killing rather than all killing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Porphyry’s treatise On Abstinence from Animal Food argues that justice extends to all sentient creatures and that the philosopher who seeks purity must refrain from killing them.
philosophy.explanation: The Neoplatonist Porphyry (3rd c. CE) built a sustained philosophical case that harming living beings is incompatible with the virtuous, god-like life.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, he makes non-killing a defining mark of virtue rather than an optional scruple.
philosophy.source: Porphyry, On Abstinence from Animal Food, Books 1–3
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the treatise’s overall argument; strong conceptual match, less aphoristic than the Kural.

kurals.tamil:
பகுத்துண்டு பல்லுயிர் ஓம்புதல் நூலோர்
தொகுத்தவற்றுள் எல்லாந் தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Pakuththundu palluyir oampudhal nooloar
Thokuththavatrul ellaam thalai.
kurals.meaning: To share one’s food with others and to protect the many forms of life is the foremost of all the virtues that the learned have gathered together in their books.
kurals.elementary: If you have a lunchbox and a hungry friend, you split your sandwich. If you see a bird with a hurt wing, you help it. Valluvar says that sharing and taking care of every living thing is the number-one rule in all the good books ever written.
kurals.university: The couplet fuses two duties — sharing food (pakuttuṇṭal) and protecting the manifold life of creatures (palluyir ōmputal) — and ranks them as “the head” (talai) of everything the authors of moral treatises (nūlōr) have compiled. Its placement in the chapter on non-killing shows that for Valluvar non-violence is not merely a prohibition but has a positive face: actively sustaining life. The appeal to the collected wisdom of the nūlōr is also a characteristic move, presenting the Kural as a distillation of an entire ethical literature. The pairing of generosity and care for life anticipates modern ethics of care that see nurture, not only abstention from harm, as the core of morality.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The devotees of the Lord are released from all kinds of sins because they eat food which is offered first for sacrifice. Others, who prepare food for personal sense enjoyment, verily eat only sin.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that food must first be offered and shared within the cycle of sacrifice; eating only for oneself is itself sinful.
hinduism.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s first half — sharing food (pakuttuṇṭal) is a central religious duty.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified on vedabase.io; matches the sharing-food theme but frames it through sacrificial offering, and does not address protecting life.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise.”
christianity.explanation: John the Baptist tells the crowds that true repentance means sharing clothing and food with those who lack them.
christianity.tie_back: Same instruction as the Kural’s pakuttuṇṭal — divide what you have to eat with those in need.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match for food-sharing; does not cover protection of all living beings.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they give food in spite of love for it to the needy, the orphan, and the captive,”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes the righteous as those who give away food they themselves desire, seeking only God’s face.
islam.tie_back: Both texts rank sharing food with the vulnerable among the highest virtues.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on quran.com; strong match for sharing, partial for the protection-of-life element.

judaism.quote_or_event: “That which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation. Go study.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel summarizes the whole Torah for a would-be convert in a single ethical principle.
judaism.tie_back: Like Valluvar ranking one virtue as the head of all that the learned have compiled, Hillel names one principle as the sum of all scripture.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; strong structural parallel (one principle as the summit of all lore), but the content is the negative golden rule rather than sharing food or protecting life.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If beings knew, as I know, the results of giving & sharing, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of selfishness overcome their minds.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that even one’s last mouthful should be shared if there is someone to receive it.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost a direct echo of pakuttuṇṭal — eating only after sharing.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified on Access to Insight; near one-to-one on sharing food, though the protection-of-life half is not in this passage.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Triptolemus, who received grain from Demeter and spread agriculture to humankind, was credited with three laws: honour your parents, honour the gods with fruits, and spare animals.
greek_mythology.explanation: Porphyry reports this Eleusinian tradition, linking the gift of shared grain with a command not to harm animals.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Combines the Kural’s two themes — sharing food and protecting living creatures — in a single mythic lawgiver.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a late report of an older tradition; good thematic fit but historically indirect.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch, in On the Eating of Flesh, protests that for the sake of a little flesh humans deprive animals of the sun, of light, and of the span of life that is theirs by nature.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch argues that sustaining our own lives does not justify cutting short the lives of other creatures.
philosophy.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s palluyir ōmputal — the duty to preserve the many lives around us.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, De esu carnium I.4 (994E)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; matches the protection-of-life half, not the food-sharing half.

kurals.tamil:
ஒன்றாக நல்லது கொல்லாமை மற்றதன்
பின்சாரப் பொய்யாமை நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Ondraaka nalladhu kollaamai matradhan
Pinsaarap poiyaamai nandru.
kurals.meaning: Not killing stands alone as the one peerless good; next after it, and following close behind, comes not lying.
kurals.elementary: Think of a race where first prize is gold and second is silver. Valluvar gives the gold medal to “never kill” and the silver medal to “never lie.” Both are winners, but not hurting any living thing comes first.
kurals.university: Here Valluvar explicitly ranks two virtues he has treated separately: kollaamai (non-killing) is good “as one” (oṉṟāka) — unique and incomparable — and poyyāmai (truthfulness, the subject of chapter 30) is good “following behind it.” This is notable because in chapter 30 he had praised truth in superlative terms; the commentators reconcile the two by saying truth is supreme among virtues of speech, but non-killing is supreme absolutely. The ordering precisely mirrors Patañjali’s list of yamas, where ahiṃsā precedes satya, and the Buddhist precepts, where abstaining from killing is first and false speech fourth. It also contrasts with Gandhi, who, while treating the two as inseparable, made Truth the end and ahimsa the means.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “ahiṃsā-satya-asteya-brahmacarya-aparigrahā yamāḥ” — non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, continence and non-possessiveness are the restraints.
hinduism.explanation: Patañjali lists the five yamas (ethical restraints) of yoga, with ahimsa first and satya second.
hinduism.tie_back: Identical ranking to the Kural: non-killing first, truthfulness immediately after.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Standard Sanskrit text of the sutra; exact same order of the two virtues.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou shalt do no murder, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness,”
christianity.explanation: When asked which commandments lead to life, Jesus lists them beginning with the prohibition on murder.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it places not killing at the head of the list, with honesty (no false witness) following.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good ordering parallel, though two other commandments intervene between murder and false witness, and no explicit ranking is stated.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who do not invoke with Allāh another deity or kill the soul which Allāh has forbidden [to be killed], except by right, and do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse.”
islam.explanation: Among the qualities of the servants of the Most Merciful, refraining from unjust killing is named immediately after refusing idolatry.
islam.tie_back: Shows unjust killing ranked among the very gravest sins, near the top of the moral order as in the Kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on quran.com; supports the high ranking of non-killing but does not pair it with truthfulness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Keep thee far from a false matter; and the innocent and righteous slay thou not: for I will not justify the wicked.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah’s law of justice places the command to shun falsehood and the command not to kill the innocent in a single verse.
judaism.tie_back: Binds together exactly the two virtues the Kural ranks — not lying and not killing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Pairs the same two virtues, but in a judicial context and without ranking them.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Pāṇātipātā veramaṇī sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi” — I undertake the training rule to abstain from taking life.
buddhism.explanation: The first of the five lay precepts is abstaining from killing; abstaining from false speech (musāvādā) is the fourth.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, non-killing is the first and foundational precept, with non-lying following among the core rules.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Standard Pali formula; non-killing is first, though lying is fourth rather than second.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod names Horkos (Oath), who most afflicts men who knowingly swear falsely, while the avenging Erinyes, born from the blood of the wounded Ouranos, punish bloodshed.
greek_mythology.explanation: Early Greek myth assigns divine punishers to both the perjurer and the shedder of blood.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows falsehood and bloodshed as twin cosmic offences, though without the Kural’s explicit ranking.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak match — no strong Greek myth ranks non-killing above truthfulness; offered as the best available parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Ahimsa and Truth are so intertwined that it is practically impossible to disentangle and separate them.”
philosophy.explanation: Gandhi likens the two to two sides of a coin, but calls ahimsa the means and Truth the end.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Gandhi ranks and pairs non-violence and truth; interestingly he inverts the Kural’s order, placing Truth highest.
philosophy.source: M. K. Gandhi, From Yeravda Mandir, ch. 2 “Ahimsa or Love”
philosophy._accuracy_note: Quote confirmed via search of the Gandhi Ashram Sevagram / mkgandhi.org editions; same pairing, opposite priority.

kurals.tamil:
நல்லாறு எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும்
கொல்லாமை சூழும் நெறி.
kurals.transliteration:
Nallaaru enappaduvadhu yaadhenin yaadhondrum
Kollaamai soozhum neri.
kurals.meaning: If you ask what is called the good path, it is the way of life that carefully considers how to avoid killing any creature whatsoever.
kurals.elementary: When you walk in a garden, you watch where you step so you don’t squash the ants or crush the flowers. Valluvar says the “good road” in life is exactly that: always looking out so that you don’t hurt even the smallest living thing.
kurals.university: The couplet defines nallāṟu, “the good path,” not by a doctrine or ritual but by a disposition: the neṟi (way of conduct) that “deliberates upon” (cūḻum) not killing “anything at all” (yātoṉṟum). The verb cūḻ suggests active, careful forethought — non-killing is not passive but a vigilant attentiveness in every act. The phrase yātoṉṟum explicitly extends the scope to all living beings, however small, aligning the Kural with the rigorous ahiṃsā of Jain and Buddhist ethics. This conception of ethics as an attentive way of moving through the world anticipates Albert Schweitzer’s “reverence for life.”

hinduism.quote_or_event: “…austerity; simplicity; nonviolence; truthfulness; freedom from anger; renunciation; tranquillity; aversion to faultfinding; compassion for all living entities…” — these “belong to godly men endowed with divine nature.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the divine qualities that lead toward liberation, including ahimsa and compassion for all beings.
hinduism.tie_back: Marks non-violence toward all creatures as a defining feature of the good, liberating path.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified on vedabase.io (excerpt); ahimsa is one quality among many rather than the definition of the path.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs identifies care for the life even of one’s animals as a mark of the righteous person.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the good way is shown by concern for the lives of all creatures, not only humans.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on extending care to animals; less absolute than the Kural’s “not any creature at all.”

islam.quote_or_event: “And there is no creature on [or within] the earth or bird that flies with its wings except [that they are] communities like you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes animals and birds as communities like human beings, all known to and gathered by God.
islam.tie_back: Grounds the Kural’s regard for “any creature whatsoever” in the dignity of all living communities.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on quran.com; supports the moral standing of all creatures but is not itself a prohibition on killing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace.”
judaism.explanation: Said of Wisdom, and applied by the rabbis to the Torah as a whole, which they held exists “for the sake of the ways of peace.”
judaism.tie_back: Defines the good path, as the Kural does, as a way of non-harm and peace.
judaism._accuracy_note: Path-as-peace imagery matches; the verse does not specifically speak of killing or of animals.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “And what, monks, is right action? Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from stealing, abstaining from unchastity: This, monks, is called right action.”
buddhism.explanation: In analysing the Noble Eightfold Path, the Buddha defines right action beginning with abstention from taking life.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly identical to the Kural: the good path (magga / nallāṟu) is defined first by not killing.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 45.8, Magga-vibhanga Sutta (Thanissaro Bhikkhu trans.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified on Access to Insight; very close structural and thematic match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Plato recalls the so-called “Orphic life” of old, in which people abstained from animal sacrifice and from everything that has life, keeping to what is lifeless.
greek_mythology.explanation: Followers of the mythic singer Orpheus were remembered for a way of life defined by refusal to kill.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An ancient Greek “good path” defined, like the Kural’s, by abstaining from killing any creature.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; good match, though Plato presents it as a historical custom rather than an endorsed ideal.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is good to maintain and cherish life; it is evil to destroy and to check life.”
philosophy.explanation: Albert Schweitzer’s ethic of reverence for life holds that every living thing has a will-to-live that the ethical person must respect.
philosophy.tie_back: A modern restatement of the Kural’s good path: careful attention never to destroy any life.
philosophy.source: Albert Schweitzer, Civilization and Ethics (The Philosophy of Civilization, Part II)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Quote confirmed via search (Wikipedia / animal-rights-library reproductions of Schweitzer); translations vary slightly.

kurals.tamil:
நிலைஅஞ்சி நீத்தாருள் எல்லாம் கொலைஅஞ்சிக்
கொல்லாமை சூழ்வான் தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Nilaianji neeththaarul ellaam kolaianjik
Kollaamai soozhvaan thalai.
kurals.meaning: Among all those who, fearing the round of worldly existence, have renounced the world, the foremost is the one who, fearing the sin of killing, carefully keeps to non-killing.
kurals.elementary: Some people give up their toys, their fancy food and their comfy beds to become monks. That’s hard! But Valluvar says the very best of them is the one who is most careful never to hurt a living thing. Being gentle matters more than giving things up.
kurals.university: Valluvar compares two kinds of fear: nilai añci — fear of the “state” of worldly existence and rebirth that drives ascetics to renounce (nīttār) — and kolai añci, fear of the guilt of killing. He declares that among all renunciants, the one moved by the second fear and who deliberates on non-killing is talai, the head. This subordinates the whole apparatus of asceticism to a single ethical commitment, a characteristic Kural move that ranks inner moral conduct over outward religious status. The same move appears in the Mahabharata’s claim that ahimsa is itself the highest penance, and in the Dhammapada’s definition of the true monk as one who has laid down violence toward all beings.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Abstention from injury is the highest religion. It is, again, the highest penance.”
hinduism.explanation: Bhishma declares that ahimsa is not only the highest dharma but also the highest form of tapas (austerity).
hinduism.tie_back: Directly supports the Kural: non-killing ranks above every other austerity practised by renunciants.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva, Section CXV (K. M. Ganguli trans.)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verbatim from Ganguli on sacred-texts.com; near one-to-one match on ranking non-injury above other penance.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul teaches that even the most extreme renunciation is worthless without love.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it subordinates outward renunciation to an inner ethical disposition — here love, there non-killing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Structural parallel (renunciation ranked below an ethical virtue); the virtue named is love, not non-killing.

islam.quote_or_event: “The cases which will be decided first (on the Day of Resurrection) will be the cases of blood-shedding.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that bloodshed is the first matter between people that God will judge.
islam.tie_back: Reflects the Kural’s kolai añci — the fear of bloodguilt as the gravest concern of a God-fearing person.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on sunnah.com; supports fear of killing as paramount, but does not compare it with renunciation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?”
judaism.explanation: After asking whether God wants thousands of rams or even one’s firstborn, Micah answers that God wants justice and mercy instead.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks ethical mercy above elaborate religious self-sacrifice.
judaism._accuracy_note: Parallel in ranking ethics above ritual/renunciation; not specifically about killing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even though he be well-attired, yet if he is poised, calm, controlled and established in the holy life, having set aside violence towards all beings — he, truly, is a holy man, a renunciate, a monk.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says the true renunciant is marked not by outward austerities but by having laid down violence toward all beings.
buddhism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural: among renunciants, the truest is the one who has renounced harming life.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified on Access to Insight; near one-to-one match (see also Dhp 141 on the futility of mere austerities).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Apollo killed the Cyclopes, Zeus required even this god to atone by serving a mortal, Admetus, as a herdsman for a year; Heracles likewise served Omphale in expiation for killing Iphitus.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth even gods and the greatest heroes had to submit to humiliating servitude to cleanse bloodguilt.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Reflects kolai añci — the dread of bloodguilt is so great that it outranks divine or heroic status.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; weak-to-moderate parallel on the gravity of killing, without the renunciant comparison.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Empedocles, in his Purifications, portrays himself as an exiled daimon and calls on mortals to cease from the harsh-sounding slaughter by which, unknowingly, they devour one another.
philosophy.explanation: The philosopher-purifier treated abstention from bloodshed as the core of the purified, god-like life.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes refusal to kill the heart of the path of spiritual purification.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of fragments; good thematic match.

kurals.tamil:
கொல்லாமை மேற்கொண் டொழுகுவான் வாழ்நாள்மேல்
செல்லாது உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Kollaamai merkon dozhuguvaan vaazhnaalmel
Sellaadhu uyirunnum kootru.
kurals.meaning: Death, the devourer of lives, will not advance upon the days of one who has made non-killing the rule of his conduct.
kurals.elementary: In old stories, Death is like a hunter who comes to take people away. Valluvar says that hunter holds back from someone who never hurts any creature — as if even Death respects a person who protects life.
kurals.university: Kūṟṟu, “the one who divides” (Yama, Death), is here personified as “the eater of lives” (uyiruṇṇum). Valluvar claims that it “will not go” (cellātu) against the life-span of one who lives by non-killing. Commentators differ: some read this literally as a promise of long life, others (like Kalaignar) as a poetic image of Death hesitating in awe, and still others spiritually, as freedom from the cycle of rebirth. The idea of karmic reciprocity — sparing life earns life — is explicit in Buddhist teaching on the karmic causes of long and short lives, and has echoes in the biblical promise of prolonged days for sparing the mother bird.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who does not seek to cause the sufferings of bonds and death to living creatures, (but) desires the good of all (beings), obtains endless bliss.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu promise unending happiness to one who never inflicts captivity or death on living beings.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it promises a reward beyond death’s reach to the one who refuses to kill.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com; good match, though it speaks of endless bliss rather than Death holding back.

christianity.quote_or_event: “What man is he that desireth life, and loveth many days, that he may see good? Keep thy tongue from evil, and thy lips from speaking guile. Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it.”
christianity.explanation: The Psalmist teaches that long and good life belongs to those who turn from evil and pursue peace.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s link between a harmless, peaceful life and many days of life.
christianity._accuracy_note: Thematic parallel (peaceable conduct and long life); not specific to non-killing.

islam.quote_or_event: “The merciful are shown mercy by Ar-Rahman. Be merciful on the earth, and you will be shown mercy from Who is above the heavens.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that mercy shown to those on earth is answered by divine mercy.
islam.tie_back: Reciprocity as in the Kural: one who spares and shows mercy to life is spared in turn.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on sunnah.com; parallel logic of reciprocal mercy, but no mention of death or long life.

judaism.quote_or_event: “But thou shalt in any wise let the dam go, and take the young to thee; that it may be well with thee, and that thou mayest prolong thy days.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah commands sparing the mother bird when taking from a nest, promising long life in return.
judaism.tie_back: Very close to the Kural: sparing animal life is explicitly rewarded with prolonged days.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the reward of long life for sparing life, though the command is limited in scope.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “…having abandoned the killing of living beings, abstains from killing living beings, lays aside the rod and lays aside the knife… If… he comes to the human state, he is long-lived wherever he is reborn.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha explains to Subha that abstaining from killing is the karmic cause of long life.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly identical to the Kural: non-killing keeps death at bay.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 135, Cula-kammavibhanga Sutta (Ñanamoli Thera trans.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified on Access to Insight; near one-to-one match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poor couple Baucis and Philemon try to kill their only goose to feed their disguised divine guests; the gods forbid its slaughter, then spare the couple from the flood and grant them to die together at the same hour.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid’s tale the gods stop the killing and reward the couple with protection from death’s disaster.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An image of divine favour holding death back from the gentle and hospitable.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the reward is for hospitality more than non-killing, so the match is partial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial, Socrates tells his judges that the gods do not neglect the good, so death holds no terror for them.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it suggests death has no real power over the one who lives rightly.
philosophy._accuracy_note: General parallel on the righteous being beyond death’s harm; not specific to non-killing.

kurals.tamil:
தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும் செய்யற்க தான்பிறிது
இன்னுயிர் நீக்கும் வினை.
kurals.transliteration:
Thannuyir neeppinum seyyarka thaanpiridhu
Innuyir neekkum vinai.
kurals.meaning: Even if it would cost you your own life, do not do the deed that takes away the precious life of another being.
kurals.elementary: Suppose a bully says, “Hurt that puppy or I’ll hurt you.” Valluvar says: don’t hurt the puppy, even if you get hurt yourself. The puppy’s life is just as sweet to it as yours is to you.
kurals.university: This is one of the most uncompromising couplets in the Kural: one must not perform “the act that removes another’s sweet life” (piṟitu iṉṉuyir nīkkum viṉai) even if it means losing one’s own. The adjective iṉ (sweet) applied to the other’s life insists on its equal preciousness. Varadarasan explicitly reads it as forbidding killing even to save oneself — a stance close to Jain absolutism and more radical than most legal traditions, which permit self-defence. The Talmud reaches a similar conclusion for the case of being forced to kill an innocent person under threat, reasoning that one cannot know one’s own blood is “redder” than another’s.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Shibi, asked by a hawk to surrender a dove that had taken refuge with him, offered his own flesh — finally his whole body — rather than let the dove be killed.
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata’s tale, the gods Indra and Agni test Shibi, who chooses self-sacrifice over allowing a life to be taken.
hinduism.tie_back: Enacts the Kural precisely: give up your own life rather than cause another being’s death.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (story of Shibi, the hawk and the dove)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; strong match (the dove is only surrendered-or-saved rather than killed by Shibi, but the principle is the same).

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.”
christianity.explanation: In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus teaches non-retaliation, accepting harm rather than inflicting it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it asks one to bear harm to oneself rather than harm another.
christianity._accuracy_note: Parallel principle of non-retaliation; does not explicitly address the case of losing one’s life.

islam.quote_or_event: “If you should raise your hand toward me to kill me - I shall not raise my hand toward you to kill you. Indeed, I fear Allāh, Lord of the worlds.”
islam.explanation: Abel (Habil), threatened with murder by his brother, refuses to kill even to defend himself.
islam.tie_back: Nearly the Kural in narrative form: better to be killed than to kill.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on quran.com; strong one-to-one match.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is preferable that he should kill you and you should not kill. What did you think, that your blood is redder and more precious than his? Perhaps that man’s blood is redder.”
judaism.explanation: Rava rules that a man ordered to kill another on pain of death must let himself be killed rather than murder.
judaism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s teaching: even to save your own life, do not take another’s.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 25b (William Davidson ed., Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; near one-to-one match (for human victims).

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says that even if bandits were to saw a monk limb from limb with a two-handled saw, one who let his mind turn to hatred would not be following his teaching.
buddhism.explanation: In the Simile of the Saw the Buddha demands non-hatred and non-retaliation even under mortal attack.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it forbids answering even a threat to one’s own life with harm to another.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase (page not retrievable at time of research); focuses on hatred as well as action.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Oedipus kills Laius at a crossroads after being struck by him on the road, yet this killing — done in what he saw as self-defence — brings pollution and plague on Thebes and ruin on himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Sophocles, a killing provoked by a threat to oneself still carries full bloodguilt.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Supports the Kural’s point that saving or defending oneself does not make killing innocent.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; partial parallel, as the tragedy turns more on unknowing parricide than on self-sacrifice.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Asked by Polus whether he would rather suffer injustice or do it, Socrates answers that he would want neither, but if forced to choose he would rather suffer it than do it.
philosophy.explanation: The exchange arises in a discussion of tyrants who kill whom they please; Socrates holds that doing wrong harms the soul more than suffering it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it prefers suffering harm — even death — to inflicting it.

kurals.tamil:
நன்றாகும் ஆக்கம் பெரிதெனினும் சான்றோர்க்குக்
கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கங் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Nandraakum aakkam peridheninum saandrorkkuk
Kondraakum aakkam kadai.
kurals.meaning: Even if the gain it brings is said to be great and good, to the noble-minded any gain that comes through killing is the lowest of things.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone says, “If you trap and kill this bird, you’ll win a huge prize.” A good person says “No, thanks.” Valluvar says a prize that costs a life isn’t a prize at all — it’s the worst kind of win.
kurals.university: Valluvar concedes his opponent’s premise — the prosperity (ākkam) gained may indeed be “great” and even called “good” — and still pronounces it kaṭai, the very lowest, in the eyes of the cāṉṟōr (the noble, perfected ones). Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read the verse as targeting Vedic animal sacrifice (vēḷvi), which promised wealth and heaven through ritual killing; the Kural thus sides with the Jain and Buddhist critique of sacrificial violence. More broadly the couplet rejects consequentialist justifications for killing: no outcome, however beneficial, can redeem the means. The same refusal to let ends justify the taking of life underlies Kant’s formula that persons may never be used merely as means.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “It would be better to live in this world by begging than to live at the cost of the lives of great souls who are my teachers. … If they are killed, everything we enjoy will be tainted with blood.”
hinduism.explanation: Arjuna, facing battle, refuses a kingdom won by killing his elders, calling such enjoyment blood-stained.
hinduism.tie_back: Arjuna voices the Kural’s judgement that gain through killing is contemptible — though Krishna goes on to overrule him on grounds of duty.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified on vedabase.io; strong match for the sentiment, but it is Arjuna’s position, which the Gita itself does not ultimately endorse.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But go ye and learn what that meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice”
christianity.explanation: Jesus quotes Hosea to teach that God desires mercy rather than ritual offerings.
christianity.tie_back: Echoes the commentators’ reading of the Kural as rejecting the promised benefits of sacrificial killing in favour of mercy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on mercy over sacrifice; does not address gain explicitly.

islam.quote_or_event: “…do not say to one who gives you [a greeting of] peace, “You are not a believer,” aspiring for the goods of worldly life; for with Allāh are many acquisitions.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids killing someone who offers peace for the sake of worldly spoils, reminding believers that God’s rewards are greater.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it condemns gain obtained through killing, however tempting.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on quran.com; good match in a battlefield context.

judaism.quote_or_event: “So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns against joining those who ambush and kill for plunder, noting that greed for gain destroys life.
judaism.tie_back: Directly condemns, as the Kural does, prosperity sought through killing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match on the moral baseness of gain through bloodshed.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Advising the brahmin Kutadanta, the Buddha describes a great sacrifice of an ancient king in which no oxen, goats, fowl or other creatures were slain, and all was offered with ghee, oil and honey; Kutadanta then releases the animals he had gathered for slaughter.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha redefines sacrifice so that its benefits come without killing.
buddhism.tie_back: Matches the commentarial reading of the Kural as rejecting the promised gains of animal sacrifice.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong match to the sacrificial reading of the couplet.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Agamemnon sacrifices his daughter Iphigenia to gain favourable winds for the fleet to Troy; the ‘gain’ is won, but the killing brings his own murder on his return.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Aeschylus the great advantage bought with a life is shown to be ruinous and shameful.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Illustrates the Kural: even a great gain won through killing is the lowest of things.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong narrative match, including the sacrificial setting.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Kant’s formula of humanity: always treat humanity, in yourself or in another, as an end, and never merely as a means.
philosophy.explanation: Kant holds that persons have dignity, not a price, so no advantage can justify sacrificing one for an outcome.
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s refusal to weigh a life against any gain, however great.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 4:429
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase (translations vary); applies to rational beings, not to all living creatures.

kurals.tamil:
கொலைவினைய ராகிய மாக்கள் புலைவினையர்
புன்மை தெரிவா ரகத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Kolaivinaiya raagiya maakkal pulaivinaiyar
Punmai therivaa ragaththu.
kurals.meaning: People who make killing their work are regarded as doers of vile deeds in the minds of those who understand what baseness truly is.
kurals.elementary: Some jobs make you proud, like helping people or growing food. Valluvar says that a job built on killing living things makes wise people think less of you, because they can see how it hardens the heart.
kurals.university: The couplet names the kolaiviṉaiyar, those whose “occupation” (viṉai) is killing, and uses the word mākkaḷ — often reserved for people who have lost human discernment — to describe them. In the minds of those who discern baseness (puṉmai terivār), they are pulaiviṉaiyar, doers of polluted, degraded work. The verse is a moral judgement rather than a caste statement, though the vocabulary of pulai (pollution) reflects the social idiom of its time and should be read critically today. Its underlying insight — that habitual killing corrodes compassion — is shared by the Buddha’s list of wrong livelihoods and by Thomas More’s Utopians, who kept citizens from butchery lest it destroy the feeling of mercy.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who permits (the slaughter of an animal), he who cuts it up, he who kills it, he who buys or sells (meat), he who cooks it, he who serves it up, and he who eats it, (must all be considered as) the slayers (of the animal).”
hinduism.explanation: Manu extends the guilt of killing to everyone in the chain of slaughter and trade.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it condemns those whose work is bound up with killing.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com; strong match on the guilt of killing as an occupation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.”
christianity.explanation: John teaches that the murderer, and even the hater, is cut off from the life of God.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s verdict that the killer is spiritually degraded.
christianity._accuracy_note: Parallel judgement on the killer’s standing; concerns murder of humans, not killing as a trade.

islam.quote_or_event: “But whoever kills a believer intentionally - his recompense is Hell, wherein he will abide eternally, and Allāh has become angry with him and has cursed him and has prepared for him a great punishment.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an pronounces a curse and severe punishment on the deliberate killer of a believer.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it marks the killer as degraded and cursed in the eyes of the just.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on quran.com; scope is intentional killing of a believer, not killing as an occupation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.”
judaism.explanation: After Cain murders Abel, God curses him to be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth.
judaism.tie_back: The first killer becomes the first outcast — the degradation the Kural attributes to killers.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good parallel on the killer’s lowered, cursed status; a single murder rather than a trade of killing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Monks, a lay follower should not engage in five types of business. Which five? Business in weapons, business in human beings, business in meat, business in intoxicants, and business in poison.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists trades that are wrong livelihood because they depend on harming or killing.
buddhism.tie_back: Directly parallels the Kural’s kolaiviṉaiyar — those whose livelihood is killing are on the wrong path.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.177, Vanijja Sutta (Thanissaro Bhikkhu trans.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified on Access to Insight; strong match on killing as a condemned occupation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ixion, remembered as the first mortal to shed kindred blood, was shunned by gods and men so completely that no one would purify him, until Zeus himself did — and Ixion later ended bound on a fiery wheel.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar makes Ixion the archetype of the killer who becomes an outcast.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows the killer as vile and shunned in the eyes of the discerning, as in the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the detail that no one would purify him comes from later mythographers (e.g. Diodorus 4.69).

philosophy.quote_or_event: In More’s Utopia, citizens are not allowed to slaughter animals themselves, because the Utopians believe that butchery gradually kills the feeling of mercy, the gentlest affection of human nature.
philosophy.explanation: Thomas More imagines a society that protects its citizens’ compassion by keeping them away from killing as a trade.
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s insight that the work of killing degrades the one who does it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong match, though Utopia assigns the task to bondsmen, raising its own moral problems.

kurals.tamil:
உயிருடம்பின் நீக்கியா ரென்ப செயிருடம்பின்
செல்லாத்தீ வாழ்க்கை யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Uyirudambin neekkiyaa renba seyirudambin
Sellaaththee vaazhkkai yavar.
kurals.meaning: The wise say that those who now live wretched, impoverished lives in diseased bodies are those who once separated life from the bodies of other beings.
kurals.elementary: It’s like planting seeds: if you plant thorns, you get thorns later. Valluvar says that hurting and killing are like planting thorn seeds — sooner or later, sickness and hard times grow back toward the one who planted them.
kurals.university: The final couplet adopts the voice of received wisdom (eṉpa, “they say”): those with diseased bodies (ceyir uṭampu) living a miserable, impoverished life (cellāt tī vāḻkkai) are those who “removed life from bodies” (uyir uṭampiṉ nīkkiyār). All the major commentators read this karmically, as the fruit of killing in a former birth. The couplet closes the chapter by grounding the ethics of non-killing in moral causation; it has parallels in Manu and in the Buddha’s teaching that harming beings leads to sickliness. Modern readers will note that such teaching can be misused to blame the sick and poor — a danger also recognised within other traditions, as when Jesus rejects the idea that a man’s blindness was caused by sin (John 9:3).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “injury (to sentient beings) is punished by general sickliness”
hinduism.explanation: In its catalogue of the bodily marks of past sins, Manu assigns chronic illness as the consequence of harming living beings, stating earlier that some suffer for crimes “committed in a former (existence).”
hinduism.tie_back: Almost identical to the Kural: harming life in a former existence yields a diseased body now.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com; near one-to-one match on karmic sickness from injuring beings.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells Peter to sheathe his sword at the arrest, warning that violence returns upon the violent.
christianity.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s principle that those who take life reap suffering in return — though within one lifetime, not across births.
christianity._accuracy_note: Parallel on retribution for violence; no doctrine of rebirth, and John 9:3 cautions against reading illness as punishment.

islam.quote_or_event: “And whatever strikes you of disaster - it is for what your hands have earned; but He pardons much.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an teaches that misfortunes are linked to one’s own deeds, though God forgives much.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it traces present suffering to past wrongdoing.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified on quran.com; general moral causation, not specific to killing or former births.

judaism.quote_or_event: “because you drowned others, they drowned you. And in the end, they that drowned you will be drowned.”
judaism.explanation: Hillel, seeing a skull floating on the water, reflects that those who kill are killed in turn.
judaism.tie_back: Expresses the Kural’s logic of measure-for-measure consequence for taking life.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified on Sefaria; strong retributive parallel, without the doctrine of rebirth.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who inflicts violence on those who are unarmed, and offends those who are inoffensive, will soon come upon one of these ten states: Sharp pain, or disaster, bodily injury, serious illness, or derangement of mind, … or loss of wealth…”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada lists the painful consequences — including illness and poverty — that befall those who harm the harmless.
buddhism.tie_back: Nearly the Kural: illness and a ruined life follow from violence against living beings (cf. MN 135 on sickliness).
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified on Access to Insight (quote abridged with ellipses); strong match.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tantalus, who in later tradition killed his son Pelops and served him to the gods, is shown by Odysseus in the underworld standing in a pool under fruit trees, forever hungry and thirsty as water and fruit recede from him.
greek_mythology.explanation: His endless deprivation is the archetypal Greek image of punishment for an abominable killing.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Mirrors the Kural’s “wretched life” of want as the fruit of having taken life.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; Homer describes the punishment but not the crime, which comes from later sources (Pindar even rejects the cannibal story).

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato cites an ancient teaching that the murderer is punished in Hades and, when born again on earth, must suffer the very thing he did, dying at the hands of another.
philosophy.explanation: In the Laws, Plato uses this tale of reincarnational justice to deter killing.
philosophy.tie_back: Very close to the Kural: killing in one life brings suffering in the next.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong match including the rebirth element.
